summary: This standards-track RFC defines a service for distributing time zone data and leap-second rules. It gives reliable, secure and fast delivery to clients such as calendar applications and operating systems.

plainLanguage.summary: Clocks in different places change on different dates. This describes a service that sends devices up-to-date time zone rules so they show the right time.

questions: how do clients get tz updates
how do clients get time zone updates
subtitle: A simple HTTP and JSON service that keeps clocks, calendars and operating systems supplied with current time zone rules.

tldr.problem: Daylight saving rules can change often and sometimes with very little notice, yet clients usually get time zone data only through slow updates such as operating system patches.
tldr.mechanism: TZDIST is an HTTP service with six actions (capabilities, list, get, expand, find, leapseconds) that return JSON metadata or time zone data. Clients sync cheaply using a synchronization token and ETags.
tldr.outcome: Clients and caching servers can discover a service by SRV, TXT or a well-known URI, pull only the zones that changed, and also fetch leap-second data. The RFC does not define where the data comes from.

facts.label: Actions
facts.value: 6: capabilities, list, get, expand, find, leapseconds

today: RFC 7808 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Time Zone Data Needs a Service
sections.content:
Time zone data typically combines a UTC offset with daylight saving time (DST) rules. The offset for a region changes infrequently, but DST rules can change often and sometimes with very little notice, maybe hours before a change takes effect.

Calendaring systems (for example those using iCalendar, RFC 5545) and operating systems rely on this data. The RFC says there had been no fast and easy way to keep it current: data often ships as files that must be compiled, and operating system changes may reach machines only with an infrequent update. Old, unsupported systems may need manual patching.

The service also covers leap seconds, which map International Atomic Time (TAI) to UTC. The protocol is based on HTTP (RFC 7230) with a simple JSON API (RFC 7159). The RFC does not define the source of the data; it assumes a reliable one exists, such as the IANA-hosted time zone database (RFC 6557).
sections.plainLanguage: Governments sometimes change when the clocks jump forward or back, and they do not always warn us early. Devices need a quick way to hear about the change instead of waiting for a big update.

sections.title: Providers and Clients
sections.content:
The service is described as layers. Contributors give information about time zones to publishers, who aggregate it, judge its reliability and generate time zone data. Root providers obtain data from one or more publishers and make it available. Secondary providers are typically simple caches of a root server, located closer to clients, that cache and periodically refresh the data and reduce the load on roots. Clients (applications, operating systems and so on) fetch from either kind of provider.

Layers may be merged: a vendor could implement everything as one monolithic virtual server. The RFC is concerned only with the protocol between providers and from provider to client. It does not define how contributors pass information to publishers, how publishers vet it, or the format publishers produce.
sections.plainLanguage: It works like a news chain. People report changes, an editor decides what is true, a main office keeps the official copy, and local branches hand out copies so the main office is not swamped.

sections.title: Zones, Aliases, Truncation and Versions
sections.content:
A time zone here is a description of the past and predicted future timekeeping of a collection of clocks that are meant to agree. It is not simply a region at one UTC offset: "Central European Time" may correspond to several zones such as Europe/Berlin and Europe/Paris. Each period with a constant UTC offset is an observance.

Zones have unique identifiers set by publishers. The RFC does not define an identifier format or a global naming scheme. Aliases map a name onto an identifier (for example US/Eastern to America/New_York), and a server must keep alias mappings and let clients query with them. Localized names (for example "Nueva York") may also be kept.

Servers may truncate data to a range, because clients may not need the distant past or far future. The start point is inclusive and the end point exclusive, both in UTC. A server that truncates MUST advertise its ranges in the capabilities response. When truncating the start of a VTIMEZONE, it MUST include exactly one STANDARD or DAYLIGHT subcomponent whose DTSTART matches the start point. When truncating the end, it MUST include a TZUNTIL property.

For versions, publishers follow a monolithic model (one version for the whole data set, such as "2015a") or an incremental model (each zone has its own version). The service must expose publisher and version per time zone, so clients can fetch only what changed.
sections.plainLanguage: A time zone is a rule book for one set of clocks. An alias is a nickname for the same rule book. Sometimes you only need the rules for a few years, so the service can send a shorter version.

sections.title: The Six Actions
sections.content:
Each action is an HTTP GET on a resource built from a URI template, and servers MUST support all of them. A service-prefix (the context path) is discovered by the client; a data-prefix may be added to partition data, but the RFC defines no partitions. Zone identifiers appear percent-encoded, so America/New_York becomes America%2FNew_York.

  • capabilities: tells the client what the server supports, including version, source, formats, truncation and the available actions.
  • list: lists all zone identifiers in summary form with publisher, version, aliases and optional localized names, plus an opaque synctoken. The optional changedsince parameter returns only zones changed since a previous token.
  • get: returns one zone as time zone data with a strong ETag. The default media type is text/calendar; iCalendar-in-XML and iCalendar-in-JSON are also available. Optional start and end truncate the data.
  • expand: expands a zone into observances between a required start (inclusive) and end (exclusive), so thin clients can find offsets without doing full expansion.
  • find: matches identifiers, aliases or localized names with a simple glob pattern where an asterisk is the wildcard. Underscores are mapped to spaces and ASCII letters to lowercase before comparing.
  • leapseconds: returns leap-second data with expires, publisher, version and a list of utc-offset and onset pairs.

Errors use a JSON problem details object (RFC 7807) whose type is a URN such as urn:ietf:params:tzdist:error:tzid-not-found. Responses MUST be UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: The service is like a help desk with six windows. One says what it can do, one lists all the zones, one hands over a zone, one works out the clock changes for a year, one searches by name, and one tells about leap seconds.

sections.title: Finding the Service and Staying in Sync
sections.content:
A client needs a host name, port and request path. The RFC offers two discovery methods. SRV records use two new service labels: timezone (HTTP without TLS) and timezones (HTTP with TLS). Clients MUST honor TTL, Priority and Weight. A TXT record with a path key can give the context path; when present, clients MUST use it. Otherwise they use the well-known URI /.well-known/timezone, which the server MUST redirect to the real context path and MUST NOT use as the endpoint itself. Other mechanisms, such as a DHCP option, could also be used.

To sync everything, a client calls list, stores the synctoken and each zone's metadata, then fetches the zone data. Later it calls list with changedsince set to the saved token, compares each returned etag with its cached ETag and uses get only for zones that differ. A client that needs one or a few zones can use a conditional get with If-None-Match; an unchanged zone gives 304 Not Modified.

Clients SHOULD poll for changes at least once a day, and a secondary provider SHOULD poll once per hour. A client with pre-provisioned data can list the metadata and fetch only zones whose publisher and version do not match.
sections.plainLanguage: First you find the help desk's address. After that you keep a receipt number from your last visit. Next time you show the receipt and only ask about what changed since then.

sections.title: JSON Responses and New iCalendar Properties
sections.content:
Section 6 defines the JSON for each action. The capabilities response has version (which MUST be 1), info and actions. Inside info, exactly one of primary-source or secondary-source is present, along with formats and optionally truncated, provider-details and contacts. Clients MUST ignore unexpected JSON members.

The list and find responses carry synctoken and a timezones array whose entries have tzid, etag, last-modified, publisher, version and optionally aliases and local-names. The expand response lists observances with a name, an onset, and utc-offset-from and utc-offset-to in seconds.

The RFC adds two iCalendar properties. TZUNTIL is an exclusive UTC upper bound on the validity of data in a VTIMEZONE, allowed zero or one time. TZID-ALIAS-OF names another zone identifier for which the main identifier is an alias, allowed zero or more times.
sections.plainLanguage: The answers come in a tidy form with named boxes, so any program can read them. Two new labels were also added to calendar files: one says how long the rules are good for, and one says what other names the zone has.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Wrong time zone data breaks local time, so servers MUST support HTTP over TLS and MAY also offer plain HTTP. Secondary servers MUST use TLS to fetch from a primary. Clients SHOULD use TLS, MUST NOT fall back to non-TLS if the TLS service is unavailable, and MUST NOT follow a redirect from a TLS service to a non-TLS one. Clients MUST verify the server's identity.

Against DNS attacks, clients SHOULD check that the SRV target is the queried domain or a sub-domain, and treat any mismatch as a failure. Servers SHOULD throttle high request rates, and MAY require authentication.

On privacy, request patterns can fingerprint clients. Suggested precautions include always using TLS, avoiding TLS session resumption, syncing the entire set of zones, randomizing fetch order, avoiding conditional requests, cookies and authenticated requests, and randomizing the poll offset. A server could insert a fake zone to track clients, which a client can detect by comparing two independent providers. The RFC notes that some of these steps make the protocol less efficient.
sections.plainLanguage: Because wrong clock rules cause missed meetings, the connection must be locked and you must check you are talking to the right server. Also, asking for just one odd zone can tell the server things about you, so careful clients ask for everything.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA created a "TZDIST Service Actions" registry, seeded with the six actions, under the policy Specification Required with a designated expert. It added the timezone well-known URI and the service names timezone and timezones, both for TCP. It also created the "TZDIST Identifiers" registry under the URN prefix urn:ietf:params:tzdist, with an IETF Review policy, holding seven error URNs: invalid-action, invalid-changedsince, tzid-not-found, invalid-format, invalid-start, invalid-end and invalid-pattern. The two new iCalendar properties are registered too.
sections.plainLanguage: Official lists were made so every action name, error code and service label has one agreed meaning.
